title: Monitoring & reporting sustainability
blurb: Describe how sustainability measures are set, monitored and reported on, from the business case to lessons learned.
question: A rail depot upgrade has a target to divert 90% of its site waste from landfill. In month four the figure drops to 78%. How should the project have set up this measure, how is it monitored and reported, and what should happen now?

teach.body: Sustainability objectives only count if someone tracks them. Monitoring means collecting data regularly and comparing it with targets. Reporting means passing the results to the people who must act on them: the project manager, the sponsor, the board and, often, the wider organisation. The measures are set in the business case and project management plan, tracked through the project's normal reporting, and reviewed at decision gates and in lessons learned.

teach.caption: The loop repeats every reporting period. Learning feeds the next project's targets.

teach.body: A sustainability measure needs a clear definition, a baseline (the starting point), a target, an owner responsible for the data, a data source and a reporting frequency. It must link to an objective in the business case, so it shows whether the promised benefit is arriving. Suppliers often provide much of the data, so reporting duties should be written into their contracts. Keep measures proportionate: a few meaningful KPIs beat dozens nobody reads.

teach.caption: Month 4 misses the target. The project manager finds a subcontractor mixing waste in one skip, adds signage and a toolbox talk, and reports the dip and the fix to the board. By month 6 the figure recovers, and the cause is logged as a lesson.

steps.label: Decision gates
steps.sub: Is the case still on track?

teach.caption: Sustainability travels through the NORMAL project reporting, not a separate silo. Forecast breaches beyond tolerance are escalated like any other.

teach.body: Standards and frameworks give structure. ISO 14001, for example, sets requirements for an environmental management system: the organisation sets environmental objectives, monitors its performance and keeps improving. Projects in such organisations use those processes and records. At each decision gate, the board checks sustainability performance alongside time, cost and benefits. At closure, results go into lessons learned so the next project sets better targets.

rows.label: Measures set
values: In the PMP, baselined at Definition
In acceptance criteria and release goals

teach.text: Exam trap: treating monitoring and reporting as the same, or as a one-off at the end. Monitoring collects and compares data regularly; reporting passes it to the people who must act. A single sustainability report at closure is too late to correct anything, and a KPI with no baseline or target cannot show progress.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say where measures are set: objectives and KPIs in the business case and project management plan, each with a baseline, target and owner.
Describe monitoring: regular data collection from meters, waste records and supplier returns, compared with targets.
Describe reporting: through normal progress reports and dashboards to the sponsor and board, with escalation beyond tolerance.
Mention standards or frameworks, such as ISO 14001.
Close the loop: review at decision gates and capture lessons learned for future projects.
Set measurable sustainability objectives and KPIs in the business case and PMP.
Each measure needs a baseline, target, owner, data source and frequency.
Monitor regularly; report through normal progress reports and dashboards to the board.
Use standards and frameworks such as ISO 14001 for structure.
Review at decision gates and capture lessons learned at closure.

summary: You can now describe how sustainability measures are set up with baselines, targets and owners, how data is collected and monitored, and how results are reported through normal project reporting to the sponsor and board. You can also explain the role of standards such as ISO 14001, decision gate reviews and lessons learned.

A.q: Where should a project's sustainability objectives and measures FIRST be set out?
options: In the lessons learned report at closure
In the supplier's final invoice and receipt
In the issue log once problems are found
In the business case and management plan
A.why: Measurable sustainability objectives belong in the business case and the project management plan, so they are agreed and tracked from the start.

whyNot.0: Lessons learned come at the end; objectives must be set at the start.
whyNot.1: Invoices record payment, not project objectives.
whyNot.2: The issue log records problems; objectives should exist before any problem arises.

A.q: What is the main difference between monitoring and reporting sustainability measures?
options: Monitoring tracks data; reporting shares it
Monitoring is optional; reporting is legal
Monitoring only ever happens after handover
Reporting is done by suppliers, not the PM
A.why: Monitoring is the regular collection and comparison of data; reporting communicates the results to those who must act on them.

whyNot.1: Both are part of good practice; neither is simply optional or simply legal.
whyNot.2: Monitoring happens throughout the project, not only after handover.
whyNot.3: Suppliers often provide data, but the project manager reports to the sponsor and board.

A.q: Which is the BEST example of a measurable sustainability KPI?
options: Be greener than our last project
Try to reduce waste where we can
Divert 90% of site waste from landfill
Show real care for the local environment
A.why: It names what is measured and sets a clear target, so progress can be tracked against it.

whyNot.0: 'Greener' is vague and has no measure or target.
whyNot.1: 'Where we can' sets no target and cannot be tracked.
whyNot.3: A worthy aim, but there is nothing to measure.

B.q: Why does a sustainability KPI need a baseline?
options: So suppliers can set their own targets
So progress can be measured against it
So the KPI never needs to be reported
So the sponsor can skip the gate review
B.why: A baseline is the starting point; without it there is nothing to compare later results with.

whyNot.0: Targets are set by the client and sponsor, not by suppliers for themselves.
whyNot.2: A baseline makes reporting meaningful; it does not replace it.
whyNot.3: Gate reviews still happen; the baseline helps them judge progress.

B.q: On the Thames depot upgrade, month 4's waste diversion falls well below the 90% target. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Wait for the closure report to mention it
Change the target to match the actual figure
Find the cause and plan corrective action
Stop collecting waste data until it recovers
B.why: Monitoring exists to trigger action: find out why the figure dropped, put a fix in place and report it.

whyNot.0: Waiting until closure means the problem continues unchecked.
whyNot.1: Moving the target hides the problem and needs proper authority anyway.
whyNot.3: Stopping data collection removes the evidence needed to manage the problem.

B.q: Through which route should sustainability performance normally be reported to the sponsor and board?
options: The normal progress reports and dashboards
A separate report issued only at closure
Informal chats with whoever is available
The supplier's own marketing materials
B.why: Reporting sustainability through normal progress reports and dashboards keeps it visible alongside time, cost and quality.

whyNot.1: A report only at closure is too late to correct anything.
whyNot.2: Informal chats leave no record and may miss the decision-makers.
whyNot.3: Supplier marketing is not an objective report of the project's performance.

C.q: An organisation is certified to ISO 14001. What does this MOST directly tell its project managers?
options: Its projects need no environmental targets
It is exempt from environmental regulation
It has published a carbon-neutral guarantee
It has an environmental management system
C.why: ISO 14001 sets requirements for an environmental management system, which projects can use to set objectives, monitor performance and improve.

whyNot.0: Certification means the organisation sets environmental objectives; projects still need targets.
whyNot.1: A standard does not exempt anyone from the law.
whyNot.2: ISO 14001 is a management system standard, not a carbon-neutral guarantee.

C.q: In an iterative project, when are sustainability measures MOST likely to be reviewed?
options: Only at the final post-project review
At each iteration review or release
Never, since the scope is allowed to flex
Only when the sponsor requests a report
C.why: Iterative projects review progress at the end of each iteration or release, which is the natural point to check sustainability measures too.

whyNot.0: Waiting until the end loses the iterative advantage of fast feedback.
whyNot.2: Flexible scope does not remove the need to measure sustainability.
whyNot.3: Reviews are built into the iterative rhythm, not left to ad hoc requests.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT good practice when monitoring and reporting sustainability?
options: Assigning an owner to each measure
Reviewing results at decision gates
Collecting data only at project close
Capturing lessons for future projects
C.why: Data must be collected regularly. Collecting it only at the end leaves no chance to correct performance.

whyNot.0: Owners make sure data is collected and acted on.
whyNot.1: Gate reviews check sustainability performance alongside the business case.
whyNot.3: Lessons learned improve future targets and methods.

reteach.title: A household cutting its energy use
reteach.question: A family wants to use 20% less electricity than last year. They have a smart meter, a shared calendar and a monthly family chat. How does that mirror monitoring and reporting a project's sustainability?

blocks.body: Last year's usage is the baseline; 20% less is the target. The smart meter collects data every day (monitoring). Each month, one person sums it up for the family (reporting). If the figure is off track, the family agrees an action, such as drying clothes outside. At the end of the year they note what worked for next year (lessons learned).

blocks.caption: Illustrative figures. The forecast shows the family is off track, which prompts action now, not at year end.

blocks.text: A smart meter nobody looks at is monitoring without reporting. The data only helps when it reaches the people who can act on it, in time to act.

explain.body: Turn sustainability objectives into KPIs in the business case and PMP. Give each one a baseline, a target, an owner, a data source and a reporting frequency.

test.q: Which set of details makes a sustainability measure usable?
options: Baseline, target, owner and frequency
Logo, slogan, colour and font choice
Supplier name, price and delivery date
Team size, location and working hours
test.why: A baseline, target, owner and frequency let the measure be tracked and acted on.

whyNot.1: Presentation details do not make a measure trackable.
whyNot.2: These are procurement details, not a measure definition.
whyNot.3: These describe the team, not a sustainability measure.

explain.body: Monitoring relies on reliable, regular data: meter readings, fuel and energy records, waste transfer notes, supplier certificates and contractor returns, compared with targets each period.

test.q: Which is the MOST reliable source for a project's site electricity use?
options: A guess by the site manager
The supplier's sales brochure
The original tender estimate
Regular meter readings
test.why: Meter readings measure actual use, taken regularly so trends can be spotted.

whyNot.0: A guess is not data and cannot be verified.
whyNot.1: A brochure describes a product, not the site's actual use.
whyNot.2: A tender estimate is a forecast, not actual consumption.

explain.body: Report sustainability through the normal progress reports and dashboards. If a measure is forecast to breach its tolerance, escalate to the sponsor, just as for time or cost.

test.q: A sustainability KPI is forecast to miss its target by more than the project manager's agreed tolerance. What should happen?
options: Quietly adjust the KPI target
Escalate it to the sponsor
Remove it from the dashboard
Delay reporting until closure
test.why: A forecast breach beyond tolerance must be escalated so the right authority can decide what to do.

whyNot.0: Changing targets quietly hides the problem and bypasses governance.
whyNot.2: Removing it from view stops decision-makers seeing the problem.
whyNot.3: Waiting until closure prevents any correction.

explain.body: Frameworks such as ISO 14001 give structure. Decision gates check sustainability alongside the business case, and lessons learned at closure improve the targets and methods of future projects.

items.label: Results and causes logged as lessons

test.q: Why should sustainability results be reviewed in lessons learned at closure?
options: To reopen the project's approved budget
To replace the business case's targets
To improve how future projects perform
To assign blame for any missed targets
test.why: Lessons learned turn this project's experience into better targets and methods for future projects.

whyNot.0: Closure is about finishing, not reopening budgets.
whyNot.1: The business case targets are not rewritten at closure; results are compared with them.
whyNot.3: Lessons learned aim to improve, not to blame.
